claims.text: Structural and chemical stability in equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles is governed by temperature-activated, element-specific diffusion.
Coupling temperature-activated diffusion with a reactive atmosphere promotes local compositional fluctuations.
Local compositional fluctuations lead to phase segregation or oxidation.
Inert environments preserve a homogeneous solid solution to higher temperatures than reactive environments.
The selected nanoparticles initially comprise five or more metals in equal or near-equal ratios and form a uniform room-temperature solid solution.
Temperature-activated diffusion preferentially produces compositional fluctuations at surfaces and grain boundaries.
Diffusion-driven compositional fluctuations cause phase decomposition or oxide formation.
At elevated temperatures, enhanced atomic mobility overcomes the mixing-entropy contribution stabilizing the solid solution.
Surface reactions in reactive atmospheres amplify atomic mobility.
Oxidation drives preferential segregation of particular metal elements.
Inert atmospheres slow diffusion, segregation, and oxidation processes.
Under catalytic reactive conditions, detectable phase segregation, oxide or secondary-phase formation, and chemical inhomogeneity will begin at lower temperatures than under inert conditions.
Under inert conditions, the solid solution will remain stable up to a higher critical temperature.
The baseline particles have no detectable phase segregation or preferential elemental oxidation.
Particle-size variation, impurities, and nonuniform initial composition may confound the stability comparison.
XRD and TEM-based characterization can distinguish relevant phase and microstructural states in high-entropy alloys.
A lack of a statistically significant atmosphere-dependent difference in segregation, oxidation, or chemical inhomogeneity would falsify the proposed reactive-atmosphere mechanism.
